summary: This Experimental document extends Bidirectional Forwarding Detection to measure BFD stability, specifically with a mechanism for detecting BFD packet loss.

eli5.summary: Two friends keep checking "you there?" and this adds counting how many checks got lost on the way.

questions: how does bfd detect packet loss
what is the bfd null auth type
subtitle: A way for BFD to count the control packets it silently misses, using a sequence number that goes up by one every time.

tldr.problem: A BFD session stays Up as long as at least one packet arrives within the Detection Time, so extra lost packets inside that window go unnoticed even when they hint at a deteriorating path.
tldr.mechanism: The receiver compares the sequence numbers of successive BFD control packets, which a meticulous authentication type increments on every packet, and counts the gaps as lost packets. A new NULL Auth Type supplies such a sequence number for sessions with no real authentication, and a YANG module exposes a stability flag and a lost-packet-count.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Experimental, and its appendix says there are no known implementations and that the authors are unsure whether a simple lost count predicts stability well enough.

today: RFC 9978, published in June 2026, is an Experimental RFC and is not on the Standards Track. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and its appendix says there are no known implementations or proof of concept.

sections.title: Why Count BFD Packet Loss
sections.content:
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD, RFC 5880) sends control packets at a high rate over the path it watches. Its Detection Time is set to the smallest feasible value so that a path failure is noticed quickly.

A BFD session remains Up as long as it receives at least one packet within the Detection Time. Other missed packets in that window are not noted by the BFD state machinery, even though they could be a useful sign of systemic issues or a deteriorating network. This RFC proposes an experimental mechanism to detect that loss. Together with the receive-packet-count from the BFD YANG model (RFC 9314), it lets operators measure the stability of BFD sessions.

The scope is limited to BFD packets. The document does not measure data traffic loss or delay on a link or tunnel.
sections.eli5: Two friends keep shouting hello to each other. They only worry if they hear nothing for a while, but this also counts the hellos that got lost, which can warn that the line is getting bad.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The example in the RFC is simple. If a receiver gets control packet k at time t, then gets packet k+3 ten milliseconds later and never sees k+1 or k+2, it has experienced packet loss that plain BFD would not report.

That information lets an implementation produce health diagnostics for each session. It could be used to act before a failure on the monitored path, by giving time for corrective action. An operator who sees a faulty path could also trigger delay and loss measurement OAM tools such as Connectivity Fault Management (Y.1731) or the MPLS packet loss and delay measurement of RFC 6374 to isolate the issue.

Stability measurement requires that a BFD Meticulous authentication type be configured.
sections.eli5: If a few of your friend's hellos go missing, you can start checking the phone line before it breaks completely.

sections.title: The NULL Auth Type
sections.content:
Loss counting needs a meticulously increasing sequence number, meaning the number goes up on every new packet sent. The authentication types that give this are Meticulously Keyed MD5 and SHA1 from RFC 5880, Meticulously Keyed ISAAC from RFC 9986, and the new NULL Auth Type defined here. NULL provides none of the protections of real authentication. It exists only to give sessions that otherwise use no authentication a sequence number for stability measurement.

The section is used when the Authentication Present (A) bit is set and the Authentication Type field contains 6. It is 8 bytes long: Auth Type, Auth Len (8), Auth Key ID, a Reserved byte and a 32-bit Sequence Number. Auth Key ID must be set to zero and ignored on receipt, and the Reserved byte must be zero on transmit and ignored on receipt.
sections.eli5: It is a numbered ticket stuck on every hello. The ticket proves nothing about who sent it, but it lets the listener see if any numbers are missing.

sections.title: How Loss Is Measured
sections.content:
The receiver counts the control packets missed during a Detection Time period by comparing the Sequence Number field in successive packets. The first BFD Authentication Section with a non-zero sequence number in a valid control packet is used to bootstrap the logic. If bfd.AuthSeqKnown is 1 and the received number is not bfd.RcvAuthSeq plus 1 in a circular number space, the loss count grows by the difference between the received number and bfd.RcvAuthSeq, and bfd.RcvAuthSeq is set to the received number. If bfd.AuthSeqKnown is 0, it is set to 1, bfd.RcvAuthSeq takes the received value and the packet is accepted.

With NULL authentication the received sequence number must not be compared with bfd.RcvAuthSeq to decide whether to discard a packet. The RFC explains why: an attacker could use an unauthenticated number to move the sequence forward, and the real neighbor's packets would then be discarded and the session would drop.

Out-of-order delivery, for example over Link Aggregate Groups (LAGs) or Equal Cost Multipath (ECMP), can make a strict comparison classify reordered packets as lost. Implementations MAY provide mechanisms so that expected packets received across an expected interval, even out of order, are not counted as lost.
sections.eli5: If you got ticket 4 and then ticket 7, you know tickets 5 and 6 went missing, so you add them to your lost count.

sections.title: The Stability YANG Module
sections.content:
The ietf-bfd-stability module augments the BFD YANG model of RFC 9314. It adds a stability boolean to single-hop, multihop, LAG and MPLS session configuration, guarded by a stability feature, and the setting is allowed only when meticulous authentication is true. It also adds a read-only lost-packet-count counter to the session statistics, which is present only if stability is configured. A null-auth identity names the new Auth Type for key chains.

The RFC's examples show a single-hop session with stability true and meticulous true, once with a SHA-1 key chain and once with the NULL algorithm. Configuring stability by any other method is out of scope, as is further analysis of the loss over time.
sections.eli5: It is a switch on the control panel that turns the counting on, and a dial that shows how many hellos were missed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using a BFD authentication mechanism that protects the packets is RECOMMENDED. The NULL Auth Type has none of the properties of authentication, so the security considerations of RFC 5880 for unauthenticated BFD all apply. Having a sequence number but no digest makes it open to injection attacks, and BFD without authentication is vulnerable to session resets.

Injected packets that do not reset the session can look like high packet loss, so sessions such as multihop paths, unauthenticated tunnels or MPLS Label Switched Paths have the same guarantees as BFD without authentication.

For the YANG module, the lost-packet-count is read-only, but the RFC notes that access to it could tell a malicious user which links are having issues, and that LAG or ECMP reordering can inflate it. Access should be restricted, for example with NACM.
sections.eli5: The numbered tickets do not stop a trickster from sliding in fake ones, so the RFC says to use a real lock when you can.

fields.desc: Length of the section in bytes.

fields.desc: Must be zero and ignored on receipt.

fields.desc: Zero on transmit, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Incremented for each successive packet sent in a session.
